summary: Islam establishes the concept of khalifah (stewardship/vicegerency) as the human role on earth — we are entrusted custodians, not absolute owners. The Quran and Sunnah prescribe care for the earth, prohibition of corruption and waste, and preservation of natural resources as religious obligations, making environmental ethics inseparable from Islamic faith.
content:
## Stewardship (Khalifah) — The Foundational Concept

'And it is He who has made you successors (khulafa') upon the earth.' (Surah al-An'am, 6:165)

'And We created from water every living thing.' (Surah al-Anbiya', 21:30)

The concept of istikhlaf (stewardship) means that humans are entrusted custodians of the earth on Allah's behalf — not its absolute owners. This theological framework makes environmental responsibility a form of worship ('ibadah) and its neglect a form of breach of trust (khiyanah).

## Prohibition of Corruption (Fasad)

Allah repeatedly condemns fasad fi al-ard (corruption on earth): 'And do not do mischief on earth after it has been set in order.' (Surah al-A'raf, 7:56)

'And when he goes away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals. And Allah does not like corruption.' (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:205)

Classical scholars (Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari) understood fasad broadly to include destruction of the natural environment, not only social corruption.

## The Sunnah on Environmental Care

**Planting trees and agriculture:**
The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If the Final Hour is approaching and one of you has a palm seedling in his hand, and he is able to plant it before the Hour comes — let him plant it.' (Musnad Ahmad, Hadith 12902; graded sahih by al-Albani)

'There is no Muslim who plants a tree or sows seeds, and a person, or a bird, or an animal eats from it, but it is regarded as a charitable gift (sadaqah) from him.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2320)

**Conserving water:**
The Prophet ﷺ performed ablution (wudu) from approximately one mudd (less than 1 litre) of water. He passed by Sa'd as he was making wudu and said: 'What is this wastage, O Sa'd?' Sa'd said: 'Can there be wastage in wudu?' He said: 'Yes, even if you are on a flowing river.' (Sunan Ibn Majah, Hadith 425; graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)

**Prohibition of pollution and waste:**
The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Removing harm from the road is a branch of faith.' (Sahih Muslim, Hadith 35)

He prohibited urinating in still water (Sahih Muslim, Hadith 281) and in places where people rest under shade (Sunan Abu Dawud, Hadith 26).

**Rules of warfare and trees:**
Classical Islamic law of warfare (siyar) prohibits cutting trees, destroying crops, and poisoning water sources — even in wartime — unless absolutely necessary. This is documented in the manuals of all four schools.

## The Concept of Hima (Protected Zones)

The Prophet ﷺ established protected wildlife reserves (hima) around Madinah and al-Naqi'. The principle was developed by the Rightly-Guided Caliphs. Classical fiqh recognises state authority to establish protected zones for environmental conservation — one of the earliest institutionalised environmental law frameworks in world history.

## Maqasid and Environment

Contemporary scholars (Ibn Ashur, al-Qaradawi) have argued that preservation of the natural environment (hifz al-bi'ah) should be included as a sixth maqsad (objective) of the Shari'ah, alongside the classical five (life, intellect, progeny, wealth, religion). This position is gaining acceptance among Islamic legal bodies.

Musnad Ahmad, Hadith 12902 — plant a tree even if Hour is coming
Sunan Ibn Majah, Hadith 425 — no wastage even on a flowing river
